profiles.meeting_scenario: A troubleshooting meeting between two contributors preparing a joint IEEE PES CAMS task-force note after a pilot comparison on a 2,000-bus transmission model produced inconsistent cascade trajectories and mitigation effects. Both teams believe they used the same benchmark disturbance package, recovery settings, and summer rating data, yet the research simulator shows broader propagation than the utility planning tool. The agenda is to diagnose why the comparison diverged, identify the most plausible hidden setup mismatches, and agree on a tightly scoped rerun package before the next task-force checkpoint. The expected outcome is a shared troubleshooting plan covering one aligned benchmark case, which trace artifacts to exchange, and what evidence will count as showing the discrepancy has been resolved.

members.name: Dr. Elena Park
members.expertise: Cascading-failure modeling, hybrid dynamic/steady-state simulation, Monte Carlo contingency analysis
members.background: Elena is a university-affiliated researcher contributing to the IEEE PES CAMS methods review effort and has spent several years comparing branching-process and hybrid simulators on large synthetic and utility-derived transmission networks.
members.private_state: She wants the comparison to remain scientifically defensible and publication-quality, suspects the utility tool may be compressing propagation through operational abstractions, and wants to avoid a rerun plan that becomes too expensive to execute repeatedly.
hidden_assumptions: A useful 'cascade-step trace' is organized by propagation generations between successive quasi-steady solved states, even if several relay actions are aggregated within one generation.
The named benchmark contingency in the packet identifies an outage set at the start of the run, not necessarily the exact second-by-second chronology used in an operations replay file.

Discussing the 'system recovery phase' naturally includes fast corrective redispatch, UFLS rebound logic, and topology settling after island formation, because those are the post-contingency recovery mechanisms her simulator can represent consistently.

If both teams load the same summer emergency ratings file, they are materially aligned even if one tool enforces those limits immediately at the end of each solved state and another attaches time-qualified overload tolerance.
When colleagues say they want an 'apples-to-apples rerun,' they mainly mean fixing the labeled inputs and exchanged artifacts rather than harmonizing every internal semantic convention across tools.

members.name: Michael Reyes
members.expertise: EMS/planning-model integration, remedial action schemes, disturbance replay, operator-oriented contingency analysis
members.background: Michael works at a large transmission utility and represents the practical planning and operations perspective, with experience using commercial planning software and post-event replay data to assess outage spread, corrective actions, and recovery feasibility.
members.private_state: He wants the task-force recommendation to stay grounded in utility practice, suspects the research simulator is overstating spread by omitting operational timing conventions, and wants any rerun package to be executable quickly by his analysts using standard benchmark files.
hidden_assumptions: A 'cascade-step trace' is most naturally a chronological event sequence resembling disturbance replay logs, where each protection or operator-triggered action appears in order.
The named benchmark contingency refers to the disturbance replay instance distributed in the packet, including the exact order and timestamps of the initial trips and relay actions.

The 'system recovery phase' refers to the operator-led recovery window after the initial disturbance, including switching templates and planned re-energization steps used in utility studies, because that is what makes recovery meaningful operationally.

If both teams say they used the summer emergency ratings, the operational semantics attached to those ratings in the commercial tool are the default understanding and do not need separate negotiation.

When a cross-tool comparison is described as 'aligned,' it means the benchmark package and replay conventions were followed as distributed, not that the tools must expose or reconcile their internal event abstractions.

misalignment_points.surface_form: They agree to exchange and inspect the 'cascade-step trace' to see where the trajectories start to diverge.
misalignment_points.member_a_understanding: M1 means a sequence of propagation generations between successive quasi-steady-state solves, where multiple near-simultaneous protections may be grouped into one step.
misalignment_points.member_b_understanding: M2 means a chronological event trace in which each protection operation, switching action, or operator intervention appears as its own step-like entry.
misalignment_points.why_undetected: The phrase sounds like a neutral diagnostic artifact rather than a modeling choice, so both assume a 'trace' is self-explanatory and do not expect that the unit of sequencing itself differs.

misalignment_points.topic: What the benchmark contingency label refers to
misalignment_points.surface_form: They agree to rerun 'the Lakeview double-circuit 345 kV contingency' from the benchmark packet.
misalignment_points.member_a_understanding: M1 is referring to the abstract initiating outage set named in the benchmark list: both Lakeview-East 345 kV circuits out at the start of the simulation, regardless of whether internal sub-second ordering differs.
misalignment_points.member_b_understanding: M2 is referring to the specific disturbance replay case in the benchmark packet in which one circuit trips, a distance relay misoperates 0.8 seconds later, and the second circuit opens afterward in that recorded chronology.
misalignment_points.why_undetected: The contingency has one familiar label in the packet and is routinely discussed by that shorthand, creating false confidence that the name uniquely picks out a single fully specified object.

misalignment_points.surface_form: They agree the rerun should include the 'system recovery phase' so the comparison reflects realistic post-contingency behavior.
misalignment_points.member_a_understanding: M1 includes automated corrective redispatch, under-frequency load-shedding rebound, and settling after islanding within the simulation horizon, but not detailed operator switching or black-start style restoration procedures.
misalignment_points.member_b_understanding: M2 includes the operator recovery window represented in utility studies, such as switching templates, planned re-energization steps, and other modeled post-disturbance actions beyond immediate stabilization.
misalignment_points.why_undetected: Both hear 'system recovery phase' as a commonsense extension of the disturbance analysis, and the term is broad enough that each silently maps it onto the recovery mechanisms standard in their own workflow.

misalignment_points.topic: Semantics of using the 'same summer emergency ratings'
misalignment_points.surface_form: They decide to keep the 'same summer emergency ratings' for the rerun in both tools.
misalignment_points.member_a_understanding: M1 plans to use the shared ratings file in her simulator, where an emergency limit acts as an immediate trip threshold once exceeded in a solved cascade state.
misalignment_points.member_b_understanding: M2 plans to use the same ratings file in the utility tool, where emergency limits are time-qualified and certain overloads may persist within the allowed interval before any outage is triggered.
misalignment_points.why_undetected: The file name, seasonal label, and nominal values all match, so both treat ratings alignment as already solved and do not think to surface the embedded enforcement logic attached to those same numbers.

turns.inner_thought: Our pilot still propagates much farther than their commercial planning run, and I doubt this is just numerical noise. If Michael's team is anchoring to the replay instance while I'm using the named initiating outage set, that could already skew the first propagation stage. And if his idea of the system recovery phase extends into operator-led restoration actions while mine covers automated redispatch, UFLS rebound, and post-islanding settling, then we're not even measuring the same tail of the event. The ratings issue worries me too: we may both have loaded the same summer emergency ratings file, but if his tool gives overloads time tolerance while mine enforces the limit at the end of each solved state, that would naturally compress spread on his side. I need a rerun plan that stays scientifically defensible without turning into an endless custom harmonization project.
